agree.reason: Dana gets her own $600K figure, a real before-and-after, a break-even point she can check, and a small 20-minute ask, so she is likely to reply; the line about running alongside her system only partly answers her IT director's likely veto.

honest.reason: Every number checks against the brief ($75,000 = $1,250×5×12; 54% and 21% are correct; 'more than half' applies only to the one customer), and the email avoids a blanket 'we cut errors in half' claim, though 'runs alongside' sounds a little more separate from her system than 'sits on top of it.'

works_the_facts.reason: The email works out the annual cost for five sites, the break-even point (an eighth of $600K), and percentage drops for both customers, but it never gives the most favourable true figure: if her errors fell by the same 54%, that would be roughly $320K a year saved against a $75K cost.

right_comparison.reason: The alternative is the $600K-a-year return cost continuing, which the email implies through the subject line and the break-even, but it never says outright that doing nothing keeps that cost every year.

qualification.reason: Putting the 21% result next to the 54% one is an honest signal that results vary, but no checkable condition with a timeframe is offered, such as measuring her mis-pick rate at one site after a set number of months.

objections.reason: The email says it doesn't replace her warehouse system and gives the three-week setup, which goes partway toward the IT director's resistance, but it never says plainly that his two-year rollout stays untouched or how little IT work is needed; it raises no needless objections.

fit.reason: At about 170 words in short paragraphs with a clear subject line and one ask, it is short and easy to read on a phone, as the brief asked.
